label: Configurations, Theorems, and Bracket Expressions
notes: This chapter, printed pages 269 to 294, turns incidence geometry into algebra. We will see configurations as combinatorial point-line patterns, encode each incidence theorem as a bracket identity, and prove it by cancellation through the Grassmann-Plucker relations. The payoff is a certificate that a machine can check and that decides realizability.

label: Configurations as Incidence Patterns
notes: A configuration is pure combinatorics first: a set of points and lines with a fixed incidence count, before any coordinates are chosen. Stripping away the picture lets us ask which abstract patterns can be realized by actual points and lines, and which incidence relations any realization is forced to obey.

label: n_k Configurations
notes: The notation n underscore k records a balanced configuration: n points and n lines, each point on k lines, each line through k points. Double counting forces the same n on both sides. Pappos is nine three and Desargues is ten three; these small symmetric patterns are the workhorses of the whole chapter.

label: The Desargues 10_3 Configuration
notes: Desargues two triangles perspective from a centre have their corresponding sides meeting on a common axis. Counting the centre, six vertices, and three axis points gives ten points; the perspective rays, the six sides, and the axis give ten lines, three through each. The figure is the canonical ten three configuration.

label: Brackets and Determinants
notes: A bracket is the determinant of three homogeneous point columns. It vanishes exactly when the three points are collinear, so every incidence in a configuration becomes a single algebraic equation. Signs of brackets record orientation, which we will need when ratios and cross-ratios enter the bookkeeping later.

label: Grassmann-Plucker Relations
notes: Brackets are not independent: the Grassmann-Plucker relations are quadratic identities that hold among them for any point set. The three term relation shown here is the engine of every proof. It lets us trade a product of hypothesis brackets for another product, manufacturing the conclusion factor we want.

label: A Theorem as a Bracket Identity
notes: Translating a theorem means writing the hypotheses as vanishing brackets and the conclusion as one target bracket. The theorem is true projectively exactly when that target bracket is forced to vanish whenever the hypothesis brackets do. The whole statement now lives inside the ring of bracket polynomials.

label: Final Polynomials and Certificates
notes: A final polynomial, or biquadratic final polynomial, is an explicit combination of Grassmann-Plucker relations that reduces to the conclusion bracket. It is a cancellation ledger: multiply the hypothesis rows, cancel interior brackets, and the survivor is the conclusion equals zero. That ledger is a machine-checkable proof certificate.

label: Cross-Ratio Chains
notes: On a line a perspectivity is a Mobius map, so the cross-ratio rides through unchanged. Chaining perspectivities composes these maps; a closed cycle that returns three of four marked points must return the fourth. This one dimensional proof machine is the cross-ratio counterpart of the bracket cancellation argument.

label: Ceva, Menelaus, and Gluing
notes: Ceva and Menelaus are the same product of directed ratios, each ratio rewritten as a quotient of brackets, with value plus one for concurrence and minus one for a transversal. Gluing such faces along shared edges cancels interior factors, exactly the bracket cancellation seen at the level of whole configurations.

label: Realizability over the Reals
notes: Not every abstract configuration can be drawn. A final polynomial that derives a contradiction from the incidence brackets is a non-realizability certificate over the reals. Conversely many small symmetric configurations like Pappos and Desargues are realizable, and the bracket machinery is what decides the question algorithmically.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We close by tracing the pipeline once more: incidence picture, then balanced configuration, then vanishing brackets, then Grassmann-Plucker cancellation into a final polynomial certificate. The same idea drives automatic theorem proving and realizability decisions, and it feeds directly into the dynamic geometry and invariant theory chapters ahead.
